recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: high_risk — Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/63 amending Annexes II and III to Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 — E171 removed from permitted food additives list
recalled_ingredients.reason: In 2021, EFSA concluded that a concern for genotoxicity of titanium dioxide (E171) particles 'cannot be ruled out' and that E171 'can no longer be considered safe when used as a food additive,' so no ADI could be established (EFSA Journal 2021;19(5):e06585). On this basis, the European Commission adopted Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/63 banning E171 as a food additive; from August 7 2022 it may no longer be added to foods or food supplements in the EU. FDA still permits TiO2 at ≤1% of food weight (21 CFR 73.575) but initiated reassessment following the EFSA opinion. IARC Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic by inhalation). Nanoparticle form (<100nm) shows greater intestinal absorption and genotoxic concern.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: A white-pigment additive EFSA ruled in 2021 could no longer be considered safe due to possible genotoxicity. Banned in EU food since 2022; still permitted in US supplements. Avoid when possible.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: EU-banned white pigment. Avoid when possible.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: contaminant_risk — FDA does not approve talc as a food additive. FDA monitors cosmetic talc for asbestos; issued multiple recalls 2019–2024 including Claire's and J&J products.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Talc used in cosmetics and other consumer products can be contaminated with asbestos, a known human carcinogen (IARC Group 1). FDA's 2019 sampling of talc-containing cosmetics found asbestos in 9 of 52 products, triggering public safety alerts and voluntary recalls coordinated with the agency. Separately, IARC has reclassified talc itself as 'probably carcinogenic to humans' (Group 2A, upgraded from 2B) when not containing asbestos, further elevating concern. The primary supplement-relevant hazard is contaminant risk — asbestos and other impurities — rather than pure pharmaceutical-grade talc per se. Many supplement manufacturers do not conduct adequate asbestos-free certificate-of-analysis testing.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: Talc used in consumer products can be contaminated with asbestos, a known human carcinogen. Presence in supplements is associated with contamination risk. Avoid affected products.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: Possible asbestos contamination. Avoid.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: high_risk — FDA Certified Color Additives list (21 CFR Parts 73, 74, 82): E153/vegetable carbon not listed. Products using it as a US food colorant are non-compliant.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Vegetable carbon (E153) is permitted as a food colour in the EU, but the US FDA has not approved any form of carbon black as a food-colouring additive. FDA's inventories of color additives for food (21 CFR Parts 73, 74, 82) do not list E153, and regulatory and scientific reviews explicitly note that 'the USFDA has not approved the use of any type of carbon black for colouring food.' As a result, there is no approved pathway for using E153 as a colour in US foods or dietary supplements — equivalent in enforcement posture to Orange B, which is restricted to sausage casings only and effectively non-lawful as a supplement ingredient.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: Vegetable-carbon color is permitted in the EU but not approved by FDA as a food color. Presence in a US supplement is associated with labeling inconsistency. Avoid.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: Not FDA-approved color in supplements. Avoid.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: not_lawful_as_supplement — FDA warning letters (multiple, 2012–2023): octopamine classified as a new dietary ingredient (NDI) per 21 U.S.C. §321(ff)(1)(F) with no NDI premarket notification on file...
recalled_ingredients.reason: FDA has issued multiple warning letters for dietary supplements containing octopamine, stating that octopamine is a dietary ingredient under 21 U.S.C. §321(ff)(1)(F) but a new dietary ingredient (NDI) with no premarket notification on file. Because FDA has no knowledge that octopamine was marketed as a dietary ingredient before October 15 1994, and no NDI notification has been submitted, supplements containing octopamine are considered adulterated under section 402(f) of the FD&C Act. In practice, FDA uses these findings to conclude that products with octopamine 'do not appear to be lawfully included in products marketed as dietary supplements' — the same enforcement posture applied to other stimulant ingredients like higenamine and hordenine HCl.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: A sympathomimetic stimulant flagged by FDA as a new dietary ingredient without a lawful safety submission. Associated with blood-pressure elevation; avoid products containing it.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: FDA-flagged stimulant. Avoid.

Peer-reviewed analyses have documented it in weight-loss and performance products, where it can cause clinically relevant increases in heart rate and blood pressure. Deterenol is prohibited in sport by WADA and is not a lawful dietary supplement ingredient.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: A beta-adrenergic stimulant found in weight-loss products. Associated with cardiovascular risk; not a lawful supplement ingredient. Stop and consult a doctor.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: Unlawful stimulant linked to heart risk. Stop.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — 21 CFR 189.140 prohibits oil of calamus and calamus-containing human food.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Calamus (Acorus calamus) oil and extracts are prohibited in human food under 21 CFR 189.140 due to beta-asarone content, which was shown carcinogenic in animal studies (NTP, 1983). FDA banned calamus as a food additive in 1968. Because dietary supplements are regulated under the FD&C Act as foods, calamus-containing supplement ingredients are treated as adulterated and not lawful for use in this pipeline.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: An oil and extract prohibited in human food under US regulation due to beta-asarone content, which is linked to cancer in animal studies. Stop and consult a doctor.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: US-prohibited botanical linked to cancer concerns. Stop.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: contaminant_risk — Not a permitted food additive or dietary supplement ingredient. EPA Group A carcinogen. Any Cr(VI) in supplements constitutes adulteration.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Chromium(VI) is an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen (inhalation — lung and nasal cancers). NTP 2008 TR-546 found clear evidence of oral carcinogenicity in rats (small intestine tumors). EU CLP Category 1A carcinogen AND 1A mutagen. EPA Group A carcinogen. Not a permitted food additive or supplement ingredient in any jurisdiction — it is a contaminant only. Any supplement containing Cr(VI) is adulterated. Mechanism: Cr(VI) crosses cell membranes via sulfate/phosphate anion transporters, undergoes intracellular reductive activation through Cr(V)/Cr(IV) to Cr(III), generating ROS, Cr-DNA adducts, DNA-protein crosslinks, and strand breaks. IMPORTANT: Chromium(III) (picolinate, polynicotinate, etc.) is the beneficial supplemental form — only Cr(VI) compounds are carcinogenic.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: A known human carcinogen via inhalation, with clear oral carcinogenicity in rodent studies. Avoid supplements without verified chromium-speciation testing.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: Carcinogenic form of chromium. Avoid untested products.

recalled_ingredients.reason: Rosabella brand Moringa dietary supplement capsules recalled due to potential Salmonella contamination; Salmonella causes salmonellosis with risk of life-threatening infection in vulnerable populations.

recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: Recalled for potential Salmonella. Stop.

recalled_ingredients.reason: Psilocin is the pharmacologically active metabolite of psilocybin. It is a serotonin 5-HT2A receptor agonist responsible for the psychedelic effects of magic mushrooms. DEA Schedule I controlled substance. While psilocybin is the prodrug found in mushrooms, psilocin itself can also appear in supplement products (either as direct extract or synthetic). Any supplement containing psilocin is an illegal controlled substance.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: The pharmacologically active metabolite of psilocybin and a DEA Schedule I substance. Its presence in a supplement is associated with illegal drug inclusion. Stop and consult a doctor.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: DEA Schedule I substance. Stop.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: controlled_substance — FDA Class I recalls (2024-ongoing). Import alerts active. Not approved as dietary ingredient.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Muscimol is the primary psychoactive compound in Amanita muscaria mushrooms. It is a potent GABA-A receptor agonist causing sedation, euphoria, altered perception, and at higher doses: seizures, loss of consciousness, and respiratory depression. The margin between psychoactive and toxic doses is narrow and highly variable. Muscimol itself (as isolated compound or concentrated extract) has been marketed in gummies and capsules, leading to the 2024 Diamond Shruumz mass poisoning event.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: A potent GABA-A agonist from Amanita mushrooms — associated with sedation, altered perception, and at higher doses seizures. Not a lawful supplement ingredient. Stop and consult a doctor.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: Psychoactive mushroom compound. Stop.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: controlled_substance — FDA Class I recalls (2024-ongoing). Import alerts active. Not approved as dietary ingredient.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Ibotenic acid is a neurotoxic amino acid found in Amanita muscaria alongside muscimol. It is an NMDA receptor agonist and glutamate analog that causes excitotoxicity. Decarboxylates to muscimol during drying/processing. The combination of ibotenic acid (excitotoxin) and muscimol (GABAergic sedative) creates an unpredictable and dangerous pharmacological profile. Ibotenic acid is used in neuroscience research to create brain lesions — its neurotoxicity is well-established.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: A neurotoxic amino acid in Amanita mushrooms that acts on NMDA receptors and can cause excitotoxic brain injury. Not a lawful supplement ingredient. Stop and consult a doctor.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning_one_liner: Neurotoxic mushroom compound. Stop.

recalled_ingredients.reason: OxyElite Pro (USPlabs) was recalled in 2013 after being linked to an outbreak of 97 cases of acute hepatitis, including three liver transplants and one death. The original aegeline-containing formulation is no longer authorized; reformulated versions sold under the OxyElite name require case-by-case evaluation.
recalled_ingredients.safety_warning: OxyElite Pro was recalled in 2013 after being linked to an acute liver injury outbreak with 97 cases, three liver transplants, and one death. Stop any remaining product and consult a doctor.
